# bssd

bssd computes the posterior probability of a safety signal from blinded
clinical trial data with the models examined by Duncan (2026) and with other
published methods for blinded data. The posterior quantities are obtained by
numerical integration instead of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, so
the results do not depend on a random seed and are fast enough for
simulation studies.

## Models and functions

| Model | Data | Function | Relative risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| BDRIBS(1) | number of subjects with the event and total exposure time | `bdribs_post()` | rate ratio |
| BDRIBS(2) | number of subjects with the event and total time at risk | `bdribs_post()` | rate ratio |
| EXP_BERN | event indicator and follow-up time of each subject | `expbern_post()` | rate ratio |
| LL_BERN | event indicator and follow-up time of each subject | `llbern_post()` | ratio of the cumulative incidences at `t_star` |

BDRIBS is the Poisson-based model of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018). With
`pt_hp = Inf`, `bdribs_post()` performs their screening analysis with a
known background rate. The results of the three functions have `print()` and
`summary()` methods.

Other functions:

- `time_at_risk()`: total exposure time and total time at risk from
  subject-level data.
- `ll_cdf()` and `ll_mu()`: cumulative incidence and location parameter of
  the log-logistic distribution.
- `sim_blinded()`: simulation of blinded trial data.
- `sim_oc()`: operating characteristics of the models by simulation.

## Further methods

| Method | Data | Function | Tested quantity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Exposure-time Poisson model (Schnell and Ball, 2016) | number of events and follow-up time of each subject | `exptime_post()` | study drug rate or rate ratio |
| Binomial model (Ball and Schnell, 2016) | numbers of subjects and of subjects with the event | `binbeta_post()` | study drug proportion or ratio |
| Meta-analysis of several studies (Goren et al., 2020) | the same, for each study | `multibin_post()` | common rate ratio |
| Canary in the coal mine (Gould and Wang, 2017) | total event count, with external control data | `canary_post()` | ratio, difference or odds ratio |
| MAP prior and mixture likelihood (Brock et al., 2023) | event indicator and time at risk of each subject, historical control arms | `mapbern_post()`, `map_beta()` | ratio of the event probabilities |
| BDRIBS monitoring (Waterhouse et al., 2022) | as BDRIBS, on grids of data and for pooled trials | `bdribs_grid()`, `pooled_ratio()` | rate ratio |

- `signal_count()`: smallest event count with a signal for a number of
  subjects (decision boundaries and control charts).
- `count_oc()`: exact probability that the event count reaches the boundary.
- `elicit_prior()`: parameters of a Gamma, Beta or lognormal prior from two
  quantiles.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("gosukehommaEX/bssd")
```

## Examples

Hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Section 4.4) has 9
subjects with the event in 540 patient-years of blinded exposure, a 2:1
randomization, and a known background rate of 0.011 per patient-year on
placebo.

```{r example-aggregate}
library(bssd)
fit <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                   pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit
```

The posterior probability of r > 1 is `r round(fit$prob, 3)`. The article
reports 0.756, computed by MCMC with the bdribs package.

The four models applied to simulated subject-level data (150 subjects, 1:1
randomization, log-logistic times to the event, analysis at week 117):

```{r example-subject}
set.seed(2026)
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(5.85, 0.8))
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
lambda_hp <- -log(1 - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8)) / 104
pt_weeks <- 75 * 104
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks,
                        df = 2),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2),
  EXP_BERN = expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                          lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2),
  LL_BERN = llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                        sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = pt_weeks / 52, df_p = 2,
                        t_star = 104)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "error")]
```

`vignette("bssd")` explains the models, the priors of this example and the
simulation of the operating characteristics. The articles
`vignette("bdribs1")`, `vignette("bdribs2")`, `vignette("expbern")` and
`vignette("llbern")` describe each model, with examples, the accuracy of the
numerical integration and the comparison with MCMC; `vignette("exptime")`,
`vignette("binbeta")`, `vignette("canary")`, `vignette("mapbern")` and
`vignette("bdribs-monitoring")` describe the further methods. The
documentation is also available at <https://gosukehommaex.github.io/bssd/>.

## Validation

```{r validation-counts, include = FALSE}
test_files <- list.files("tests/testthat", pattern = "^test-.*[.]R$",
                         full.names = TRUE)
n_blocks <- sum(vapply(test_files, function(f) {
  sum(grepl("^\\s*test_that\\(", readLines(f)))
}, integer(1)))
count_judgements <- function(dir, pattern) {
  files <- list.files(dir, pattern = pattern, full.names = TRUE)
  rows <- lapply(files, function(f) {
    j <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)$judgement
    n <- table(factor(j, levels = c("PASS", "EXPLAINED", "FAIL", "INFO")))
    data.frame(file = basename(f), PASS = n[["PASS"]],
               EXPLAINED = n[["EXPLAINED"]], FAIL = n[["FAIL"]],
               INFO = n[["INFO"]])
  })
  do.call(rbind, rows)
}
judgements <- rbind(
  count_judgements("inst/reproduce/results", "^reproduce_.*[.]csv$"),
  count_judgements("inst/validation/results", "^validate_.*[.]csv$"))
```

- `tests/testthat` has `r length(test_files)` test files with
  `r n_blocks` `testthat::test_that()` blocks. Their expected values were
  computed beforehand by independent Python implementations
  (`inst/validation/python`).
- [`inst/reproduce`](https://github.com/gosukehommaEX/bssd/tree/main/inst/reproduce)
  reproduces the numerical results of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), Duncan
  (2026), Schnell and Ball (2016), Gould and Wang (2017), Brock et al.
  (2023), Goren et al. (2020) and Waterhouse et al. (2022): tables, worked
  examples and simulations.
- [`inst/validation`](https://github.com/gosukehommaEX/bssd/tree/main/inst/validation)
  compares `bdribs_post()` with the bdribs package, `expbern_post()` and
  `llbern_post()` with MCMC in JAGS, the default integration grids with finer
  grids and with an independent Python implementation, and `sim_oc()` with
  an independent Python simulation. The further methods are compared with
  independent Python computations and with MCMC in JAGS.

Each item is judged as PASS (agreement within the tolerance), EXPLAINED (a
difference whose reason is registered), FAIL (a difference without a
registered reason) or INFO (no value to compare with):

```{r validation-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(judgements, row.names = FALSE)
```

The reasons for the EXPLAINED items are listed in
[`inst/reproduce/results/SUMMARY.md`](https://github.com/gosukehommaEX/bssd/blob/main/inst/reproduce/results/SUMMARY.md).

## References

Ball, G. and Schnell, P. M. (2016). Blinded safety signal monitoring for the
FDA IND reporting final rule. In J. Lin et al. (eds.), *Statistical
Applications from Clinical Trials and Personalized Medicine to Finance and
Business Analytics*, ICSA Book Series in Statistics, 201-209. Springer,
Cham. <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-42568-9_17>

Brock, K., Chen, C., Ho, S., Fuller, G., Woolfolk, J., McShea, C. and
Penard, N. (2023). A Bayesian method for safety signal detection in ongoing
blinded randomised controlled trials. *Pharmaceutical Statistics*, 22(2),
378-395. <https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2278>

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using
alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. *Journal of
Biopharmaceutical Statistics*, 36(2), 227-244.
<https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532>

Goren, E., Lin, L.-A., Blaustein, R. O. and Ball, G. (2020). Bayesian
meta-analysis of safety outcomes using blinded clinical trial data.
*Therapeutic Innovation & Regulatory Science*, 54, 1557-1565.
<https://doi.org/10.1007/s43441-020-00183-7>

Gould, A. L. and Wang, W. B. (2017). Monitoring potential adverse event rate
differences using data from blinded trials: the canary in the coal mine.
*Statistics in Medicine*, 36(1), 92-104. <https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.7129>

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian
detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data.
*Pharmaceutical Statistics*, 17(6), 823-834.
<https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898>

Schnell, P. M. and Ball, G. (2016). A Bayesian exposure-time method for
clinical trial safety monitoring with blinded data. *Therapeutic Innovation
& Regulatory Science*, 50(6), 833-838.
<https://doi.org/10.1177/2168479016656702>

Waterhouse, B., Hartford, A., Mukhopadhyay, S., Ferguson, R. and
Hendrickson, B. A. (2022). Using the Bayesian detection of potential risk
using inference on blinded safety data (BDRIBS) method to support the
decision to refer an event for unblinded evaluation. *Pharmaceutical
Statistics*, 21(2), 372-385. <https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2175>
